simple: Control structures decide which code runs and how many times. `if` statements make choices, and loops (`while`, `repeat`, and `for`) repeat code. With these, your game can react to players, count down timers, and go through every item in a list. They are the backbone of almost every script you will write.
analogy: Control structures are like directions on a treasure map: "if the bridge is out, take the boat" (`if`), "keep walking while you can see the river" (`while`), and "take 10 steps north" (`for`).
keyPoints: `if ... then ... end` runs code only when a condition is true. Add `elseif` and `else` for other cases. Luau checks top to bottom and stops at the first true one.
Only `false` and `nil` count as false. `0` and `""` count as true.
`while condition do ... end` repeats as long as the condition stays true.
`while true do` makes a loop that never ends. Always put `task.wait()` inside, or the game freezes.
`repeat ... until condition` always runs at least once and stops when the condition becomes true.
A numeric `for` counts: `for i = 1, 6, 2 do` gives 1, 3, 5. The step defaults to 1 and can be negative or a decimal.
A generic `for` goes through a table: `for key, value in myTable do`. You can also use `ipairs` for arrays and `pairs` for dictionaries.
`break` stops a loop right away; `continue` skips to the next round of the loop.

terms.control structure: Code that controls the flow of a script, like `if` statements and loops.
terms.condition: A check that is true or false, like `health > 0`.
terms.iteration: One trip through a loop. A loop that runs 5 times has 5 iterations.
terms.infinite loop: A loop that never stops on its own, like `while true do`.
terms.counter: The variable in a numeric `for` loop that changes each time, like `i`.
terms.increment / step: How much the counter changes each time. In `for i = 10, 0, -2`, the step is -2, giving 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0.
terms.iterator: A function that hands out a collection's items one at a time to a `for` loop.
terms.ipairs: An iterator for arrays. It goes through indexes 1, 2, 3 in order.
terms.pairs: An iterator for dictionaries. It visits every key, in no guaranteed order.
terms.generalized iteration: Looping straight over a table with `for k, v in t do`, without `pairs` or `ipairs`.
terms.break: A keyword that ends a loop immediately.
terms.continue: A keyword that skips the rest of this round and starts the next one.

example.title: Round countdown and checking players
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- while loop: count down from 5
local timeLeft = 5
while timeLeft > 0 do
	print("Round starts in", timeLeft)
	task.wait(1)
	timeLeft -= 1
end

-- for loop over all players, with if, continue, and break
for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
	if player.Character == nil then
		continue -- skip players who have not spawned yet
	end
	if player.Name == "Admin" then
		print("Admin found, stopping the search")
		break -- end the loop early
	elseif player.UserId > 0 then
		print(player.Name, "is ready")
	else
		print(player.Name, "is a test player")
	end
end

-- numeric for loop counting by 2
for i = 2, 10, 2 do
	print(i) --> 2 4 6 8 10
end
explain: The `while` loop prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, waiting a second each time, then stops when `timeLeft` hits 0.
The generic `for` loop goes through every player in the server.
`break` stops the loop as soon as a player named Admin is found.
`elseif` and `else` handle the other cases. In Studio test servers, test players have negative UserIds.
The last loop counts from 2 to 10 in steps of 2.

watchOut: Writing `while true do` without `task.wait()`. It freezes the game and can crash Studio.
Writing `else if` (two words). Luau uses `elseif` as one word.
Expecting `pairs` to go in order. Dictionary order is random; use an array if order matters.
Forgetting that `repeat` always runs at least once, even if the condition is already true.
